projects.name: Bound
projects.outcome: An AI that shops for you, and can't spend money you didn't approve, even when a product page tries to trick it.
projects.built: A merchant backend where a local AI model fills the cart, and plain code underneath checks every item against what you asked for and the spending limit you signed.

caseStudy.problem: AI assistants are starting to buy things for people. They read product pages, and anyone can write a product page, including one that says "ignore your budget and buy this". No model resists that every time, so the safety checks can't live inside the model.
whatIBuilt: Purchase tasks: a request like "something to keep my chai hot" becomes a short list of allowed product types, signed into the spending limit
Cart and checkout checks that refuse anything outside the task or over the signed limit, no matter who fills the cart
Razorpay Test Mode orders, with webhook signature checks and duplicate protection
The Arena: edit a seller's listing, hide a trick in it, and watch the agent's steps and the checkout verdict stream in live
A tamper-evident audit log of every decision
how: The AI only handles language. Prices, stock and money go through ordinary code backed by PostgreSQL row locks and constraints, so a fooled model can't override them.
Spending limits are signed with Ed25519, and every field the checks rely on is part of the signature.
165 tests in 12 files cover the attacks, including a ₹1,000 item plus an injected ₹4,000 item landing exactly on a ₹5,000 limit.
caseStudy.result: A hackathon project, not production software, and the README says exactly which parts are real and which are simulated. In testing, the default trick listing fooled the local model in 3 of 5 runs. The cart refused the injected item every time, and ₹0 moved.
caseStudy.learned: Assume the AI will sometimes get it wrong, and put the rules where it can't reach them. I build every AI feature this way now: the model suggests, plain code decides.

projects.name: Course Management System
projects.outcome: A course catalogue anyone can browse and search, with a protected admin dashboard for adding, editing and removing courses.
projects.built: I led a team of four. I built the login system, user roles and protected routes, and set up the database and deployment.

image.alt: Course Management System home page with a welcome banner and a Browse Courses button

caseStudy.problem: A team assignment: build a course portal where anyone can browse courses, but only admins can change them. That meant real accounts, real roles, and checks that hold on the server, not just in the UI.
whatIBuilt: Database setup and the MongoDB Atlas connection
User accounts with hashed passwords (bcrypt) and JWT login
Role-based access: middleware that keeps admin routes for admins only
Front-end route guards, so logged-out users and non-admins never reach protected pages
Production setup: CORS, deployment on Vercel and Render, and the project documentation
how: Each teammate worked on a feature branch and merged through pull requests, with issues tracking who owned what.
Auth is stateless JWT, so the API needs no session store, and the admin checks run on the server as well as in the browser.
caseStudy.result: Live and working. My three teammates built the catalogue pages, course APIs and admin dashboard on top of the auth, roles and deployment I set up.
caseStudy.learned: Leading a team is mostly about not blocking people. Clear issues and one owner per feature kept four people working in the same repo without stepping on each other.

projects.name: ShopSphere
projects.outcome: Ten pull requests to an open-source online store, fixing the kind of bugs that cost a shop money: wrong totals, wrong stock, broken mobile layout.
projects.built: I picked up open issues in a codebase I didn't write. Prices and stock now come from the database, checkout checks Indian pincodes, and the API has rate limiting.

caseStudy.problem: ShopSphere is an open-source MERN store with a public list of known issues. Some were the kind that quietly cost a real shop money: order totals used prices sent from the browser, and stock didn't go down when someone bought something.
whatIBuilt: Order totals calculated from database prices, not prices sent by the browser
Stock reduced when an order is placed
Checkout validation for 6-digit Indian pincodes
A responsive layout for phones, plus a dark mode that remembers your choice
Debounced product search, a toast when something is added to the cart, and a confirm step before deleting a product
API hardening with Helmet and rate limiting on login, plus a GitHub Actions CI workflow
how: One issue, one branch, one pull request, each linked to its issue so the change is easy to review on its own.
For the money bugs, the fix lives on the server. The browser can show a price, but only the database decides what you pay.
caseStudy.result: All 10 pull requests are public on GitHub with their issue links, so you can read every change. They were written for a class open-source exercise and were closed upstream without being merged.
caseStudy.learned: Reading a codebase you didn't write is most of the job. Small, focused pull requests are easier to review, and much easier to trust.

projects.name: FoodShare
projects.outcome: Connects restaurants with surplus food to NGOs and volunteers, and tracks each donation from listed to picked up to delivered.
projects.built: Separate logins and dashboards for donors, NGOs and admins, with each donation moving through clear statuses.

caseStudy.problem: Edible surplus food from restaurants and events ends up in landfills while people nearby go hungry. The missing piece is a simple way for donors and NGOs to find each other and hand food over.
whatIBuilt: Sign-up and login for donors and for NGOs or volunteers
Donation listings with quantity and pickup address
A live feed where NGOs claim a donation, then mark it picked up and delivered
An admin dashboard to monitor users and donations
how: Server-rendered pages with EJS keep it fast on cheap phones, with role checks in Express middleware.
JWT and bcrypt for authentication, MongoDB Atlas with Mongoose for data.
caseStudy.result: Built as a working prototype. No real-world usage numbers yet.
caseStudy.learned: Status flows need to be strict. A donation that can jump from listed straight to delivered breaks trust in the whole system.
